timecoded_text_to_speech.text: I mean, Manga really started, I think, again, as going back to this idea of telling a story,
of having, you know, the process of when you grow up, you start to understand how not in control of your life you can be,
and how much life is a struggle for you.
And sort of this idea of struggle came into being, and I sort of was attracted to the idea of these characters that come in to play in Manga,
rebelling against the forces. So it's really a story, Manga's really a story about,
not just downstairs, it's a story about ten servants in the basement of a house, struggling against a very cruel mistress, trying to set themselves free.
That was the basis of it, but the way that I build the movement really is like a script.
I try to build gestural language that fits the story, that fits the character, that is really kind of like a dialogue that you have in theater.

That's how I build most of my works. And the music, you know, it's a long process of research, of taking an idea, and trying to really bring the different scenes and story with the scenes to come to a full evening.
I think, you know, it's really the moral of Manga is not to accept your fate, and to always fight and never give up fighting for what you believe is right.
And that's really what most of my pieces are about on some level, but it's really kind of at the heart of Manga itself.

And that's, you know, on the level of kind of a message, on the level of the dance, it's really about treating from, for me, the importance of Manga's work is to try and, at least when I'm teaching it, to really try and treat the dancers as actors, not as bodies on the stage, but as full human beings that bring every part of their being into the character that they're playing on stage.
So that, for me, is what I try to achieve there, and I hopefully will repeat it in the future works.
But it's been really great, so thank you. I hope it was okay.

youtube_description:
Interview with Choreographer Barak Marshall about his piece "Monger". More info : http://bit.ly/1nMObYU

Directed and Filmed by : Niels Plotard

"Pour Monger, pourquoi avez-vous choisi ces mouvements présents dans la pièce en particulier ?"

"Avec Monger on revient à cette idée de raconter une histoire. En grandissant on se rend compte à quel point il est difficile de contrôler sa vie, et combien la vie peut être une lutte. Cette idée de lutte a donc pris vie, et j'étais attiré par l'idée des personnages de Monger, qui se rebellent contre le pouvoir. Monger est vraiment une histoire de « Upstairs, Downstairs », (à l'étage et en bas), 10 domestiques qui se trouvent dans le sous-sol de la maison, et qui sont en opposition avec la maîtresse cruelle de la maison. Ils essaient de se libérer, c'était le fond de la pièce ; la manière dont j'ai bâti le mouvement est vraiment semblable à un scénario. J'essaie de construire un langage gestuel qui correspond avec l'histoire, avec les personnages, vraiment comme un dialogue au théatre. C'est ainsi que je construis la plupart de mon travail, c'est un long processus de recherche, où je prends une idée et je vois comment les différentes scènes et histoires peuvent aboutir à un ballet-soirée."
